title: Audit Exporter: Load + Backpressure Experiments (SRE notes)
content:
Doc purpose
- Capture what we’ve learned from load + backpressure experiments for the SIEM-ready audit export beta exporter.
- Focus areas: synthetic audit event generation realism, queue sizing/limits, downstream throttling behavior (Splunk HEC / Datadog Logs), and recommended defaults for beta.
- Audience: SRE + exporter devs + observability folks. This is NOT a customer-facing doc.

TL;DR (current recommendations)
1) Backpressure controls
- Enable max-lag safety auto-pause by default for beta tenants.
- Default max_export_lag: 30m (soft alert at 10m, page at 30m). See SLO doc for exact alert policies.
- When downstream errors persist (429/5xx), prioritize controlled lag growth over retry storms.

2) Batch sizing (starting points)
- Splunk HEC: batch_max_events=200, batch_max_bytes=800KB, flush_interval=1s.
- Datadog Logs intake: batch_max_events=100, batch_max_bytes=500KB, flush_interval=1s.
- S3: batch_max_events=1,000, batch_max_bytes=8MB, flush_interval=5s (plus partitioning).

3) Retry/backoff
- Splunk 429: exponential backoff with jitter starting 1s -> max 60s; add per-token circuit breaker after N consecutive 429s (N=10 suggested).
- Datadog 429/503: exponential backoff with jitter starting 1s -> max 60s; pause tenant export if sustained > 15m and lag approaching max.

4) Queue sizing / retention assumptions
- Target “buffer for downstream outage” for beta: 2 hours of typical tenant peak event throughput.
- Use checkpointed offsets + DLQ to preserve at-least-once semantics without infinite retries.

Open questions (need answers before GA, not necessarily beta)
- How do we communicate “auto-paused due to lag safety” in Console in a way that doesn’t look like data loss?
- Do we want an explicit per-destination ‘max outstanding bytes’ to prevent one noisy tenant from impacting shared infra?
- For Datadog: what is the tightest practical mapping between our event categories and customer-defined facets without exploding cardinality?

---

Background + setup

Exporter architecture context (as tested)
- Work queue: exporter internal queue + per-destination adapter queueing (exact backing store depends on env; tests used the current default in staging).
- Semantics: at-least-once delivery. Downstream dedup expected via event_id.
- Checkpointing: per destination + tenant scoped.
- Failures: retry with backoff; after exceeding retry policy, batch goes to DLQ and export continues (subject to safety gates).

Environments
- Staging cluster: us-east-1 staging, 3 exporter replicas unless noted.
- Downstream stubs:
  - Splunk: local HEC sandbox + throttling proxy (to inject 429, latency, connection resets).
  - Datadog: stub intake endpoint with configurable 429 and 5xx, plus optional hard request size limits.
  - S3: real S3 bucket in test account + failure injection via IAM deny / KMS misconfig (for “hard fail” paths).

Synthetic audit event generation
Goal: approximate “bursty” audit workloads, not uniform token streams.

Method
- Generator emits Audit Event Schema v2-ish payloads with stable event_id, timestamp, actor, action, resource, tenant/workspace.
- Distributions used in v1 runs:
  - Baseline: 50 events/sec steady
  - Bursty: 10x burst for 30s every 10m
  - Incident-style: 30x burst for 3m every 30m (simulates role changes + API key rotation + repeated auth failures)

Event size assumptions
- Typical event JSON: 0.8–1.6KB
- Large event JSON: up to 6KB (e.g., more resource fields; still within PII policy limits)
- NOTE: Do not generate payloads containing prohibited sensitive fields. We used placeholders for IP/user agent where present.

Event category mix (approx)
- 45% auth/session
- 20% workspace/admin config changes
- 20% API key / token events
- 10% model endpoint/config changes
- 5% “other”

Notes
- The exporter behavior is sensitive to payload size variance (compression helps Splunk; less so for Datadog if they enforce limits post-decompression).
- Bursts are more representative than steady state because downstream limiters (429) tend to kick in during bursts.

---

Experiments

Experiment 1: Baseline throughput (no throttling)
Purpose
- Establish stable throughput and baseline lag under “healthy downstream” conditions.

Config
- 3 exporter replicas
- Splunk destination only, no 429
- batch_max_events=250, flush_interval=1s

Results (high level)
- Export lag: ~0–2s steady
- CPU: moderate on exporter, with occasional spikes during flush
- No DLQ events

Observations
- Larger batch_max_events improves efficiency but increases worst-case “replay duplicate volume” when a batch fails late (trade-off for at-least-once).

Conclusion
- Baseline path OK; we should tune to reduce blast radius of any single failed batch while maintaining efficiency.


Experiment 2: Splunk HEC throttling behavior (429)
Purpose
- Understand exporter behavior under Splunk 429 responses and confirm backoff prevents retry storms.

Setup
- Splunk HEC throttling proxy returning:
  - 429 for 50% of requests for 10 minutes
  - then 429 for 100% of requests for 5 minutes
  - then recovery
- Event rate: 200 events/sec steady + bursts
- Two configs tested:
  A) aggressive batching: 500 events/batch
  B) moderate batching: 200 events/batch

Key metrics we watched
- exporter_delivery_success_total (by destination)
- exporter_adapter_http_status_total{status="429"}
- exporter_retry_queue_depth
- exporter_lag_seconds (p50/p95)
- exporter_tenant_paused_total

Results summary
- Config A (500/batch)
  - fewer requests overall, but each failed request “holds” more events.
  - lag growth steeper during 100% 429 period.
  - more painful replay when unpaused (burst of duplicates downstream unless dedup is perfect).
- Config B (200/batch)
  - more requests, but smoother lag growth and smaller replay batches.
  - overall system stabilized faster after recovery.

Notable behaviors
- Without a circuit breaker, we still see “hot loop” patterns if backoff resets on partial successes.
- Per-token circuit breaker (added in exporter PRs) significantly reduces wasted attempts during hard throttling.

Takeaway
- For Splunk HEC we should default to smaller batches than “max efficiency” to reduce replay/dedup blast radius.

Recommendation (Splunk)
- batch_max_events=200
- batch_max_bytes=800KB
- flush_interval=1s
- backoff: base 1s, max 60s, jitter on
- circuit breaker: open after 10 consecutive 429s; half-open probe every 30s


Experiment 3: Datadog intake limits (403/429/size)
Purpose
- Validate behavior under common failure modes: API key scoping mistakes (403), rate limiting (429), transient 5xx.

Setup
- Datadog stub configured for:
  - 403 for first 2 minutes (simulates bad key)
  - then 429 for 15 minutes (simulates rate limiting)
  - then 503 spikes (10% for 10 minutes)
- Event rate: 150 events/sec + bursts

Results
- 403 path:
  - Retries do not help; exporter should treat as “hard fail” and pause destination quickly.
  - Current behavior: after X attempts exporter flags destination unhealthy; needs to clearly surface “auth error” vs “throttling” in status.
- 429 path:
  - Backoff worked, but lag climbed quickly during burst windows.
  - Smaller batches were more stable.
- 503 path:
  - Backoff fine; recovered without pausing.

Recommendation (Datadog)
- batch_max_events=100
- batch_max_bytes=500KB
- flush_interval=1s
- On 403/401: pause destination immediately (or after 3 attempts) + mark as “Auth error; action required”
- On sustained 429 (> 15m): consider tenant-level auto-pause if lag > 10m and growing

Notes on mapping/cardinality
- Be careful with tagging:
  - Good: category, action, tenant/workspace id (as low-card tag), destination name
  - Avoid: resource names, user emails, raw IP/user-agent as tags (PII + cardinality)


Experiment 4: Queue sizing and recovery behavior
Purpose
- Determine minimum queue depth / buffering strategy to handle downstream outages without data loss (within retention/backfill semantics).

Setup
- 1h downstream outage (100% 429) then recovery
- Workload: 100 events/sec steady; bursts 10x every 10m

What we saw
- Queue depth grows linearly with sustained downstream failure.
- Recovery window (“time to catch up”) depends on:
  - max allowed throughput to destination (rate limiting)
  - batch sizing
  - whether we allow “catch-up mode” to exceed normal request rate (we currently do NOT, which is safer for customers)

Rule of thumb
- Buffer_needed_events ~= outage_duration_sec * avg_events_per_sec
- Buffer_needed_bytes ~= Buffer_needed_events * avg_event_size_bytes

Example sizing (single tenant)
- avg 100 events/sec, avg 1.2KB/event
- 2h buffer
- events: 100 * 7200 = 720,000 events
- bytes: ~864MB (uncompressed JSON)
- NOTE: this is only the payload; overhead for indexes/checkpoints/etc also exists.

Recommendation
- For beta, we should aim for “2 hours typical peak” buffering per tenant, but enforce global caps so a single tenant can’t exhaust shared resources.
- Enforce “max outstanding bytes” per tenant per destination (implementation detail; if not implemented, we need operational guardrails + alerting).


Experiment 5: Max-lag safety (auto-pause) + operator workflow
Purpose
- Validate that max-lag safety prevents runaway queue growth and makes operator response straightforward.

Setup
- Downstream outage (100% 429) with max_export_lag configured to 30m
- Observe:
  - When tenant export pauses
  - What metrics fire
  - How easy it is to unpause safely

Findings
- Auto-pause triggered near threshold as expected.
- Biggest operator pain point: distinguishing “paused by safety” vs “paused due to auth misconfig” quickly.
- Unpause behavior after outage:
  - If we unpause immediately at recovery, we see a “catch-up wave” that can re-trigger throttling.
  - Better: staged unpause or keep backoff state/circuit breaker state through pause/unpause.

Operational recommendation
- Preserve backoff/circuit breaker state across pauses for the destination.
- Add runbook step: validate downstream health (manual test connection) before unpause.

---

Recommended defaults (beta)

Destination adapter defaults
1) Splunk HEC
- batch_max_events: 200
- batch_max_bytes: 800KB
- flush_interval: 1s
- request_timeout: 10s
- max_in_flight_requests: 4 (per tenant per destination)
- retry_backoff: exp+jitter (1s -> 60s)
- circuit breaker: enabled; open after 10 consecutive 429; probe every 30s

2) Datadog Logs
- batch_max_events: 100
- batch_max_bytes: 500KB
- flush_interval: 1s
- request_timeout: 10s
- max_in_flight_requests: 4
- retry_backoff: exp+jitter (1s -> 60s)
- on 401/403: pause destination and require credential rotation

3) S3
- batch_max_events: 1000
- batch_max_bytes: 8MB
- flush_interval: 5s
- partitioning: by tenant + date/hour (and optionally destination)
- retries: exp+jitter (2s -> 120s) on transient S3 errors; hard fail on access denied

System safety defaults
- max_export_lag: 30m
- soft alert: 10m
- DLQ enablement: ON
- DLQ replay tooling: gated/controlled (avoid replay storms)

What to expose in Console (minimum viable for beta)
- Per destination:
  - status: healthy / degraded / paused
  - last_success_at
  - last_error (category + short message)
  - current lag
  - retrying? (yes/no)
  - paused_reason: auth_error | throttling | safety_max_lag | operator_action

---

Metrics + alerting notes (what mattered in experiments)

Most useful signals
- exporter_lag_seconds{tenant, destination} p50/p95
- exporter_adapter_http_status_total{destination, status}
- exporter_delivery_success_total / exporter_delivery_failure_total
- exporter_paused_total{reason}
- exporter_dlq_enqueued_total
- exporter_queue_depth_events / exporter_queue_depth_bytes

Cardinality warning
- tenant+destination labels are already high cardinality; avoid adding action/resource labels to metrics.

Paging guidance (beta)
- Page for:
  - lag > 30m for any beta tenant destination (unless in known maintenance window)
  - sustained 5xx to ALL destinations (indicates exporter systemic issue)
- Ticket-only for:
  - intermittent 429s where lag < 10m and stable
  - single tenant auth error (unless enterprise escalates)

---

Runbook deltas (things to add)
- Add a clear decision tree:
  1) Is it auth? (401/403) -> pause + notify customer to rotate credentials
  2) Is it throttling? (429) -> check backoff/circuit breaker; do not unpause prematurely
  3) Is it exporter-side? (5xx, timeouts, queue depth exploding) -> consider kill switch / reduce concurrency
- Add a “safe unpause” procedure:
  - verify downstream health
  - unpause 1 tenant at a time if multi-tenant incident
  - monitor lag slope and 429 rate for 10 minutes

---

Action items
- [SRE] Confirm recommended defaults with exporter team (tie to config flags) (Owner: Rafael, Target: 2025-05-06)
- [Exporter] Ensure pause reason is surfaced via status endpoint so Console can show it (Owner: Logan/Caleb partnership, Target: 2025-05-10)
- [Exporter] Preserve backoff/circuit breaker state across pause/unpause (Owner: exporter dev, Target: TBD)
- [SRE] Update SLO doc with explicit beta paging policy for sustained 429 vs lag thresholds (Owner: Sean, Target: 2025-05-08)
- [Docs/CS] Add internal guidance: “at-least-once; downstream dedup by event_id; during throttling expect lag not loss” (Owner: Colin, Target: 2025-05-12)

Appendix A: Quick reference table (defaults)
Destination | batch_max_events | batch_max_bytes | flush_interval | notes
Splunk HEC | 200 | 800KB | 1s | 429 heavy; circuit breaker
Datadog Logs | 100 | 500KB | 1s | treat 403 as hard fail
S3 | 1000 | 8MB | 5s | partition + checkpoint

Appendix B: Failure injection recipes (used)
- 429 throttle: return 429 for N% of requests; vary by 10m blocks
- latency: add 500ms–2s p95 latency for 10m to simulate network congestion
- connection reset: 1% of requests drop connection mid-stream
- auth: 401/403 for 2m, then success (validates detection + customer workflow)

Appendix C: Notes on “missing events” reports
- In tests, most “missing” reports mapped to one of:
  - lag during throttling (customer expects real-time)
  - downstream dedup or indexing delay
  - paused destination due to safety
- For support: first check lag + paused_reason + last_success_at; then check DLQ counts.
